title: Sanofi agrees to acquire Insmed for US$41B to expand respiratory medicines portfolio | HealthCare Middle East & Africa - No.1 Health & Pharma Manufacturing Industry Publication
summary: Under the agreement, Sanofi will pay US$175 per share, representing a 17.5% premium over Insmed's closing share price on November 23.

contentHtml:
USA—Sanofi has agreed to acquire US biopharmaceutical company Insmed for US$41 billion in cash, in its largest acquisition in more than two decades, as it seeks to strengthen its respiratory medicines portfolio and replenish its drug pipeline.

Under the agreement, Sanofi will pay US$175 per share, representing a 17.5% premium over Insmed’s closing share price on November 23.

The transaction will be financed through a combination of debt and existing cash, with committed financing already secured.

It follows Sanofi’s US$65 billion merger with Aventis in 2004.

The acquisition represents a major strategic move under CEO Belén Garijo, who took over in April 2026 with a mandate to improve the company’s growth prospects amid concerns about vaccine sales and pipeline development.

Following the announcement, Sanofi shares rose 5.6% at market open on November 24.

Citi analysts described the transaction as strategically sound but questioned whether Insmed’s research and development capabilities would sufficiently strengthen Sanofi’s internal pipeline.

They also raised concerns about the potential impact of the acquisition on Sanofi’s capacity for further mergers and acquisitions.

Commercial medicines strengthen respiratory portfolio

The acquisition will add two marketed therapies to Sanofi’s portfolio.

These are Brinsupri (brensocatib), an oral treatment for non-cystic fibrosis bronchiectasis (NCFB), and Arikayce (amikacin liposome inhalation suspension), an inhaled antibacterial medicine for certain patients with Mycobacterium avium complex (MAC) lung disease.

Brinsupri, a once-daily inhibitor of dipeptidyl peptidase 1 (DPP1), has been approved in several markets, including the US, European Union and Japan.

The medicine generated US$1.09 billion in revenue through September 2026, making it a blockbuster product within its first year of launch.

GlobalData forecasts that its worldwide sales could exceed US$6 billion by 2032.

Meanwhile, Arikayce generated US$433.8 million in 2025, representing 19% growth compared with the previous year.

It is the only approved inhaled therapy specifically indicated for treatment-refractory MAC lung disease patients in the US, EU, and Japan.

Pipeline assets support long-term growth strategy

Beyond its marketed products, Sanofi will acquire Insmed’s clinical pipeline, including treprostinil palmitil inhalation powder (TPIP), a once-daily inhaled prostanoid being evaluated in Phase III trials for pulmonary hypertension and interstitial lung diseases.

Sanofi expects TPIP to become a potential growth driver beyond 2030, depending on clinical results and regulatory approvals.

The programme could expand the company’s presence in rare respiratory diseases and provide additional revenue streams.

The acquisition also supports Sanofi’s efforts to diversify revenue ahead of potential competition for Dupixent (dupilumab), its leading immunology medicine developed and commercialised with Regeneron.

The drug generated €5.7 billion (US$6.2 billion) in sales in the third quarter of 2026, representing growth of nearly 35%.

However, its anticipated loss of US market exclusivity in 2031 could expose Sanofi to biosimilar competition.

In October, Sanofi and Regeneron expanded their research partnership through an agreement worth up to US$8 billion to develop four additional antibody therapies.

The Insmed transaction, which has received approval from both companies’ boards, is expected to close in the first half of 2027, subject to shareholder and regulatory approvals.

Sanofi expects the acquisition to contribute positively to earnings per share by the end of 2028 and generate annual cost exceeding US$500 million.
